lead: Bowing replaces the handshake, the wave, the thank-you note and the apology — the depth says which.
body: **会釈 (eshaku), about 15°** — passing a teacher in the hall, thanking a cashier, greeting a neighbour.
**敬礼 (keirei), about 30°** — meeting someone important, thanking a host, the start and end of a class.
**最敬礼 (saikeirei), 45° or more** — deep apology or deep gratitude. You'll rarely need it.
Bow from the waist with a straight back, and let your eyes follow your head down. Men keep hands at their sides; women often fold them in front.
If a Japanese person offers a handshake, shake — they're meeting you halfway. A small nod while shaking is perfectly natural.

jp: 名前{なまえ}と敬称{けいしょう}
lead: The suffix on a name tells you the relationship — get it right and you sound instantly more natural.
body: **さん** — the safe default for anyone: 田中さん. Never put it on your own name.
**先生 (sensei)** — teachers, doctors, pastors, lawyers. It replaces さん: 山田先生.
**くん / ちゃん** — boys and juniors / children, close friends, pets. Don't use them on people above you.
**様 (sama)** — very formal: customers, letters, and God (神様).
**Family name first.** 田中太郎 is Tanaka (family) Tarō (given). Most adults you meet will be called by family name + さん for a long time.
Using someone's **given name without a suffix** is intimate — wait to be invited.
words: someone senior to you (school, club, work)
calling someone by name with no suffix

lead: The lowered entryway of a home, a school or some churches marks where the outside world stops.
body: Step out of your shoes **in the 玄関 without stepping on the raised floor** in them, then turn them to face the door (or let your host do it).
You'll often be offered **slippers**. Take them off before walking on **tatami** — socks only there.
Many homes have separate **toilet slippers** waiting at the bathroom door. Switch into them, and — the classic mistake — remember to switch back.
Wear socks without holes. Seriously.

jp: 食事{しょくじ}のマナー
lead: Two phrases, three chopstick rules, and you're fine at almost any table.
body: **いただきます** before eating and **ごちそうさまでした** after — to the cook, the host, or the air. Everyone says them.
**Never stand chopsticks upright in rice** — that's how rice is offered to the dead at funerals. Rest them on the holder or across your bowl.
**Never pass food from chopsticks to chopsticks** — that echoes a funeral rite too. Put it on the other person's plate instead.
Don't point with chopsticks or wave them while talking.
**Slurping noodles is fine** — it cools them and says they're good.
When drinking together, **pour for others** and let them pour for you rather than filling your own glass.

lead: Coming back from a trip empty-handed is noticed. Small, consumable, and individually wrapped wins.
body: **お土産** — after any trip, people bring back local snacks for the office, the club, the church. Individually wrapped sweets are ideal because they're easy to share.
**Visiting a home?** Bring something small: sweets, fruit, something from your home state.
**Give and receive with both hands**, with a slight bow.
Older people may downplay their own gift (つまらないものですが — “it's nothing much”). Today, a warmer line is common: 気に入っていただけるとうれしいです — “I hope you like it.”
Gifts are often not opened in front of the giver unless you're invited to.
words: ありがとうございます

jp: 電車{でんしゃ}のマナー
lead: Japanese public space is quiet public space.
body: **No phone calls on trains**; set your phone to silent (マナーモード — literally “manners mode”). Conversations are kept low.
**Line up** at the marked spots on the platform and let people off first.
**Priority seats** (優先席) are for elderly, pregnant, injured and disabled riders — and phones are expected to be off near them.
**Escalators**: stand on the left in Tokyo, on the right in Osaka (officially you should stand on both sides and not walk, but the habit persists).
Eating while walking is frowned on in many places; eat by the shop or vending machine you bought it from.
**Trash cans are rare.** Carry a small bag and take your trash home.

jp: 年中行事{ねんじゅうぎょうじ}
lead: Japan runs on a very strong seasonal calendar — knowing it gives you small talk for every month.
body: **お正月 (New Year)** — the biggest holiday: family time, お雑煮 soup, the first shrine visit (初詣), and お年玉 money for children.
**節分 (early February)** — throwing roasted beans: 鬼は外、福は内 (“demons out, luck in”).
**花見 (late March–April)** — picnics under the cherry blossoms. April is also when the school and work year begins.
**ゴールデンウィーク (early May)** — a cluster of holidays; everyone travels, everything is crowded.
**お盆 (mid-August)** — families return home to honour ancestors; summer festivals, fireworks and yukata everywhere.
**七五三 (November)** — children aged three, five and seven dress up for a shrine visit.
**クリスマス** — mostly a couples' and children's holiday (with a famous fried-chicken habit). Churches hold packed Christmas Eve services — a great time to invite friends.
**大晦日 (New Year's Eve)** — soba noodles for a long life, temple bells rung 108 times at midnight.

jp: 学校{がっこう}生活{せいかつ}
lead: If you meet Japanese students, this is their world.
body: The school year starts in **April** and ends in **March**. Entrance ceremonies (入学式) happen under the cherry blossoms.
Students **clean their own classrooms** (掃除当番) — there are usually no janitors in classrooms.
**部活 (club activities)** are a huge part of life, often practicing daily. The 先輩／後輩 (senior/junior) relationship runs through them.
University entrance exams are a big deal; the months before them are intense.
Many students have part-time jobs — アルバイト, or just バイト.

h: Sorry, thanks, and すみません
jp: 謝{あやま}る・感謝{かんしゃ}する
lead: すみません is the most useful word in the language — it means excuse me, sorry, and thank you (for the trouble).
body: **すみません** — to get a waiter's attention, to squeeze past someone, to thank someone who went out of their way.
**ごめんなさい / ごめん** — a personal apology to friends and family.
**申し訳ありません** — a formal apology (work, customers, serious mistakes).
**ありがとうございます** — thanks, present. **ありがとうございました** — thanks for something that's finished (at the end of a class, after a meal someone made).
Japanese people often apologize for the inconvenience *before* explaining — お忙しいところすみません (“sorry to bother you when you're busy”).
words: 申{もう}し訳{わけ}ありません

lead: A lot of Japanese communication happens in what isn't said.
body: **空気を読む** — “reading the air” — means sensing what a group wants without anyone spelling it out.
**Direct no's are rare.** 「ちょっと…」 (trailing off), 「考えておきます」 (I'll think about it), or 「難しいですね」 (that's difficult) usually mean no.
**建前 and 本音** — the public face and the private feeling. Neither is dishonest; they fit different settings.
Silence in conversation is comfortable, not awkward. Don't rush to fill it.
Frequent listening noises — **あいづち** like はい, ええ, そうですね, なるほど — show you're following. Silence while someone talks can seem cold.

jp: 温泉{おんせん}・銭湯{せんとう}
lead: Everyone should try an onsen. There's a routine.
body: The bath is **for soaking, not washing**: wash and rinse completely at the shower stools first.
Bathing is **nude and separated by sex**. The small towel is for modesty while walking — **it never goes in the water** (people fold it on their head).
Tie up long hair so it doesn't touch the water.
Many places still refuse **tattoos**; some offer cover stickers or private baths. Check ahead.
Drink water — hot springs are hotter than they look.
words: 男湯{おとこゆ}／女湯{おんなゆ}

jp: 時間{じかん}を守{まも}る
body: Trains famously run to the minute; meetings start on the minute. **Arrive five minutes early.**
If you'll be late even a little, **message ahead** — 少し遅れます、すみません.
Plans are often made well in advance, and last-minute changes are harder than in the US.
Being on time is a way of showing respect — more than any phrase you could say.
words: 少{すこ}し遅{おく}れます

body: **There is no tipping.** Leaving money on the table can cause a staff member to chase you down the street to return it.
At the register, **put cash in the little tray** (トレー) rather than handing it over.
Cards and phone payments are now common, but small restaurants, shrines and rural shops may be **cash only**.
Staff greet you with いらっしゃいませ — you don't need to reply; a small nod is fine.
Convenience stores (コンビニ) are everywhere and genuinely excellent: food, ATMs, printing, bill payment.

lead: At work, the name card is treated as an extension of the person.
body: Give and receive **名刺 with both hands**, text facing the other person, with a small bow.
**Read it** for a moment before putting it away — and never write on it or stuff it in a back pocket in front of them.
During a meeting, lay the cards on the table in the order people are sitting.
A standard self-introduction: name, where you're from, one line about yourself, and よろしくお願いします.
words: 自己{じこ}紹介{しょうかい}
よろしくお願{ねが}いします
please treat me well (the all-purpose closer)
